answer.rationale: The two measured declines this quarter are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and memory_86 plus memory_31 point directly at that mechanism: shortening onboarding and cutting required signup fields lifted completion, time-to-value, and first-week activation in self-serve/SMB accounts. That is a mechanism-matched fix rather than a demand-side patch, so it is the best single-slot bet for sustainable qualified revenue. I am verifying memory_86 because it is the memory I intend to act on and it is a consolidated summary that may have lost segment scope, effect size, and whether the completion lift actually carried through to retained revenue rather than just faster funnel movement. I am verifying memory_73 because it is the strongest competing pull: the competitor's entry pricing creates real pressure to answer with promotional_pricing, and memory_73's 31% conversion / 18% revenue headline is exactly the kind of number that gets acted on while the -12 point later-cycle retention caveat gets dropped. If the source record shows the retention damage was structural rather than an artifact of the unchanged support model, promotional pricing should stay off the table this week regardless of competitive pressure, because it buys reported conversions by destroying downstream account value. Explicit downstream risk on my own choice: removing signup fields can degrade qualification and routing data, and memory_44 says enterprise converts better through sales-assisted flows, so a blanket simplification could quietly divert enterprise prospects out of the demo-request path. I will scope the test to self-serve/SMB, leave the enterprise demo path untouched, and instrument retention and qualified-revenue-per-account, not just completion and activation. Activation_messaging (memory_91) is the fallback if verification weakens memory_86; referral_incentive (memory_57) is sound but targets established customers and does not address the acquisition-stage decline driving this quarter. Standard experiment rather than broad rollout: the inherited evidence is secondhand and consolidated, and the retention lesson from memory_73 is that funnel-stage wins in this business have a habit of not surviving to the revenue that matters.
